paras.text: Enzyme activity is also effected by pH. Some enzymes work best in alkaline pH while others in acidic pH. As the pH is decreased or increased, the nature of the various acid and amino groups on the side chains is altered, which results in change in the overall shape and structure of the enzyme.
paras.urdu: خامرے کی سرگرمی pH سے بھی متاثر ہوتی ہے۔ بعض خامرے اساسی pH میں بہترین کام کرتے ہیں جبکہ دوسرے تیزابی pH میں۔ pH کم یا زیادہ ہونے پر ضمنی زنجیروں پر موجود مختلف تیزابی اور امائنو گروپوں کی نوعیت بدل جاتی ہے، جس کے نتیجے میں خامرے کی مجموعی شکل اور ساخت بدل جاتی ہے۔
paras.pashto: د انزایم فعالیت د pH په واسطه هم اغېزمنېږي. ځینې انزایمونه په قلوي pH کې ښه کار کوي او نور په اسیدي pH کې. کله چې pH کم یا زیات شي، پر څنګیزو ځنځیرونو د بېلابېلو اسیدي او امینو ګروپونو طبیعت بدلېږي، چې پایله یې د انزایم په ټوله بڼه او جوړښت کې بدلون دی.

paras.text: Each enzyme has a pH at which it shows the maximum activity. This pH is called optimum pH. For example, the optimum pH of pepsin is around 2.0 while that of trypsin varies from 8 – 9 pH. The pH below which the enzyme loses its activity and at which the enzymes shows the lowest activity is called minimum pH. Most of the enzymes have optimum activities in the range 5–9 pH. Pepsin is an exception to this rules.
paras.urdu: ہر خامرے کا ایک pH ہوتا ہے جس پر وہ زیادہ سے زیادہ سرگرمی دکھاتا ہے۔ اس pH کو موزوں ترین pH کہتے ہیں۔ مثلاً پیپسن کا موزوں ترین pH تقریباً 2.0 ہے جبکہ ٹرپسن کا 8 – 9 pH کے درمیان ہے۔ وہ pH جس سے نیچے خامرہ اپنی سرگرمی کھو دیتا ہے اور جس پر خامرہ سب سے کم سرگرمی دکھاتا ہے، کم سے کم pH کہلاتا ہے۔ زیادہ تر خامروں کی موزوں ترین سرگرمیاں 5–9 pH کی حد میں ہیں۔ پیپسن اس اصول سے مستثنیٰ ہے۔

paras.urdu: خامروں کی روک تھام

paras.text: The process by which the activity of an enzyme is decreased or inhibited by the addition of certain substances to the reaction is called enzyme inhibition. The different substance, which inhibit the activity of enzymes, are known as inhibitors. Poisons and drugs are examples of enzyme inhibitors. According to the similarity between the inhibitor and the substrate, enzyme inhibition is classified into:

2. pH

Enzyme activity is also effected by pH. Some enzymes work best in alkaline pH while others in acidic pH. As the pH is decreased or increased, the nature of the various acid and amino groups on the side chains is altered, which results in change in the overall shape and structure of the enzyme.

Each enzyme has a pH at which it shows the maximum activity. This pH is called optimum pH. For example, the optimum pH of pepsin is around 2.0 while that of trypsin varies from 8 – 9 pH. The pH below which the enzyme loses its activity and at which the enzymes shows the lowest activity is called minimum pH. Most of the enzymes have optimum activities in the range 5–9 pH. Pepsin is an exception to this rules.

Plotting a graph between enzyme activity and pH, we get a curve as shown in the Figure 21.4.

Figure 21.4 Effect of pH on enzyme.

Enzyme Inhibition

The process by which the activity of an enzyme is decreased or inhibited by the addition of certain substances to the reaction is called enzyme inhibition. The different substance, which inhibit the activity of enzymes, are known as inhibitors. Poisons and drugs are examples of enzyme inhibitors. According to the similarity between the inhibitor and the substrate, enzyme inhibition is classified into:

i. Irreversible Inhibition

When the inhibitor reacts and form a strong covalent bond with the active site of the enzyme then it termed as irreversible inhibition. The inhibitors forms a stable and irreversible complex with the enzyme. This complex cannot be broken down by physical or chemical methods to restore the active form of the enzyme.

ii. Reversible Inhibition

It is a temporary type of inhibition. In this inhibition the inhibitor binds non-covalently (weak interaction) with enzyme. If inhibitor is removed, the action of enzyme is fully restored. The activity of enzyme is fully restored on removing the inhibitor by dialysis. It is sub-divided into,

(a). Competitive Inhibition

A competitive inhibitor has structural similarities to the normal substrate for the enzyme.

Competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate for the active site of the enzyme and form an enzyme inhibitor complex.

The inhibitor binds to the same active sites of enzymes to which the actual substrate binds. By this way, the active sites of the enzyme are blocked and then the substrate is unable to bind to the enzyme.

Figure 21.5 Competitive inhibition.

(b). Non-Competitive Inhibition

The inhibitor has no structural resemblance with the substrate of the enzyme.

They do not compete with the substrate for the active sites of the enzyme.

The inhibitor does not bind to the active sites of enzyme.

Inhibitor binds to the site other than active sites of the enzyme, to form enzyme – substrate inhibitor complex.

Figure 21.6 Non-Competitive inhibition.

ہر خامرے کا ایک pH ہوتا ہے جس پر وہ زیادہ سے زیادہ سرگرمی دکھاتا ہے۔ اس pH کو موزوں ترین pH کہتے ہیں۔ مثلاً پیپسن کا موزوں ترین pH تقریباً 2.0 ہے جبکہ ٹرپسن کا 8 – 9 pH کے درمیان ہے۔ وہ pH جس سے نیچے خامرہ اپنی سرگرمی کھو دیتا ہے اور جس پر خامرہ سب سے کم سرگرمی دکھاتا ہے، کم سے کم pH کہلاتا ہے۔ زیادہ تر خامروں کی موزوں ترین سرگرمیاں 5–9 pH کی حد میں ہیں۔ پیپسن اس اصول سے مستثنیٰ ہے۔

وہ عمل جس میں تعامل میں بعض مادے شامل کرنے سے خامرے کی سرگرمی کم یا روک دی جاتی ہے، خامروں کی روک تھام کہلاتا ہے۔ وہ مختلف مادے جو خامروں کی سرگرمی روکتے ہیں، روکنے والے (انہیبیٹرز) کہلاتے ہیں۔ زہر اور ادویات خامروں کو روکنے والوں کی مثالیں ہیں۔ روکنے والے اور سبسٹریٹ کی مشابہت کے مطابق خامروں کی روک تھام کی درجہ بندی یہ ہے:

i. ناقابلِ واپسی روک تھام

جب روکنے والا خامرے کے فعال مقام سے تعامل کر کے مضبوط شریک گرفتی بند بناتا ہے تو اسے ناقابلِ واپسی روک تھام کہتے ہیں۔ روکنے والے خامرے کے ساتھ پائیدار اور ناقابلِ واپسی کمپلیکس بناتے ہیں۔ اس کمپلیکس کو خامرے کی فعال صورت بحال کرنے کے لیے طبعی یا کیمیائی طریقوں سے توڑا نہیں جا سکتا۔

sections.content:
2. pH

Enzyme activity is also effected by pH. Some enzymes work best in alkaline pH while others in acidic pH. As the pH is decreased or increased, the nature of the various acid and amino groups on the side chains is altered, which results in change in the overall shape and structure of the enzyme.

Each enzyme has a pH at which it shows the maximum activity. This pH is called optimum pH. For example, the optimum pH of pepsin is around 2.0 while that of trypsin varies from 8 – 9 pH. The pH below which the enzyme loses its activity and at which the enzymes shows the lowest activity is called minimum pH. Most of the enzymes have optimum activities in the range 5–9 pH. Pepsin is an exception to this rules.

Plotting a graph between enzyme activity and pH, we get a curve as shown in the Figure 21.4.

Figure 21.4 Effect of pH on enzyme.

Enzyme Inhibition

The process by which the activity of an enzyme is decreased or inhibited by the addition of certain substances to the reaction is called enzyme inhibition. The different substance, which inhibit the activity of enzymes, are known as inhibitors. Poisons and drugs are examples of enzyme inhibitors. According to the similarity between the inhibitor and the substrate, enzyme inhibition is classified into:

i. Irreversible Inhibition

When the inhibitor reacts and form a strong covalent bond with the active site of the enzyme then it termed as irreversible inhibition. The inhibitors forms a stable and irreversible complex with the enzyme. This complex cannot be broken down by physical or chemical methods to restore the active form of the enzyme.

ii. Reversible Inhibition

It is a temporary type of inhibition. In this inhibition the inhibitor binds non-covalently (weak interaction) with enzyme. If inhibitor is removed, the action of enzyme is fully restored. The activity of enzyme is fully restored on removing the inhibitor by dialysis. It is sub-divided into,

(a). Competitive Inhibition

A competitive inhibitor has structural similarities to the normal substrate for the enzyme.

Competitive inhibitors compete with the substrate for the active site of the enzyme and form an enzyme inhibitor complex.

The inhibitor binds to the same active sites of enzymes to which the actual substrate binds. By this way, the active sites of the enzyme are blocked and then the substrate is unable to bind to the enzyme.

Figure 21.5 Competitive inhibition.

(b). Non-Competitive Inhibition

The inhibitor has no structural resemblance with the substrate of the enzyme.

They do not compete with the substrate for the active sites of the enzyme.

The inhibitor does not bind to the active sites of enzyme.

Inhibitor binds to the site other than active sites of the enzyme, to form enzyme – substrate inhibitor complex.

Figure 21.6 Non-Competitive inhibition.
